title: Problem-solving therapy for pregnant women experiencing depressive symptoms and intimate partner violence: A randomised, controlled feasibility trial in rural Ethiopia.

relevance.population: Pregnant women with depressive symptoms and past-year IPV.
relevance.exposureEvidence: Pregnant 12–34 weeks, depressive symptoms PHQ-9≥5 plus functional impact and past-year IPV by non-graphic or WHO screen; psychological/emotional IPV qualifies.
relevance.rationale: Explicit domestic/intimate-partner violence exposure in the studied population; psychological intervention is within Language scope.
relevance.transferLimit: See limitation and quality fields; no population-wide clinical recommendation is implied.

age.reportedRange: Eligibility≥16 years; arm medians 25–25.5 years. Actual minimum/maximum and count under 18 not reported.
age.youthScope: Adolescent eligibility is not proof of enrolled adolescent participants; no adolescent-specific outcomes.

setting: Bu’i primary hospital and Kela health centre, rural Sodo district, Ethiopia; recruitmentApril–May 2021.

sampleSize.description: Final 25 PST-IPV/12 standard PST/15 enhanced usual care. Only 35 entered intended three-arm allocation (25/5/5); 17 psychological/emotional-IPV women were wrongly routed to linked two-arm table. Follow-up 19/25, 8/12, 12/15.

intervention.description: Four-session problem-solving therapy adapted with trauma/IPV-informed training, risk awareness and avoidance of victim blaming; sessions address participants’ chosen problems.
intervention.dose: Four sessions within 8 weeks; mean session durations approximately 32–51 minutes. 19/25 completed all 4; 5 attended none, 1 attended one.
intervention.provider: Six trained antenatal-care providers for PST-IPV, separately trained from six standard PST providers; psychiatrist/psychologist training and supervision with audio-sampled fidelity assessment.

comparator: Four-session standard PST (12 women) or enhanced usual care (15 women: well-being leaflet and local support information). All arms additional to routine antenatal care. Shared comparator structure with linked depression feasibility trial.

outcomes.name: Implementation feasibility
outcomes.result: 52 eligiblewomen enrolled; 39/52 completed assessment; delivery feasible with changes required to randomization, provider skills and scheduling.
outcomes.uncertainty: Primary aim was feasibility, not powered comparative efficacy.

outcomes.name: Acceptability and delivery fidelity
outcomes.result: 19/25 PST-IPV and 8/12 standard PST completed all 4 sessions. Providers sometimes ignored IPV disclosures; risk/confidentiality discussion needed improvement.
outcomes.uncertainty: IPV was infrequently discussed and then for 1–4 minutes. Completion alone does not establish competent IPV response.

outcomes.name: Depressive symptoms and IPV
outcomes.result: Descriptive symptoms/IPV scores fell in several arms; no powered causal comparison or effect size established.
outcomes.effectEstimate: Follow-up medianPHQ-9: 6 PST-IPV, 6 standard PST, 4 enhanced usual care in the full sample; these are descriptive medians with unequal selected follow-up denominators.
outcomes.uncertainty: No significant-benefit claim. IPV recall windows overlapped; misallocation confounds group comparison.

outcomes.name: Safety
outcomes.followUp: During trial and births by data-collection end
outcomes.result: One serious adverse event: assault by husband. Two obstructed/prolonged-labour complications among 29 participants who had delivered.
outcomes.uncertainty: Assault arm and relatedness to participation not reported; incomplete obstetric follow-up. Safe-delivery conclusion is not zero-harm evidence.

finding: PST-IPV was implementable with adaptations, but serious allocation errors, 25% missing follow-up and short descriptive assessment preclude an efficacy conclusion. One serious assault event was reported without arm or causal attribution.
limitation: Seventeen women with psychological/emotional IPV had no chance of assignment toPST-IPV; baseline imbalance suggests possible nonrandom allocation. Twelve of 39 assessments occurred before 9 weeks. Underpowered feasibility, missing follow-up, provider fidelity problems and overlapping IPV recall periods limit interpretation.

design.type: Randomized controlled feasibility study with material allocation-protocol deviations
design.randomizationEvidence: Independent statistician generated 3-arm 2: 1: 1 table; coordinator/research assistant retained tables and received calls after baseline. Enrollment in an arm closed at 25. Seventeen of 52 women misclassified as no IPV were instead allocated by linked trial’s 2-arm table, excluding their opportunity forPST-IPV; authors note possible nonrandom allocation from baseline imbalance.

masking.participants: No participant masking procedure established; active sessions versus leaflet care differ.
masking.providers: Explicitly unmasked; separate provider groups trained for each active intervention.
masking.assessors: Independent collectors exchanged recruitment sites for follow-up and were masked, with unmasking incidents to be documented; no incident count reported.

design.crossRationale: Random tables and controlled allocation are verified, but one third were routed through the wrong allocation scheme. Retain one design cross with this prominent qualification; no double-blind claim and no reliable efficacy inference.

quality.riskOfBias: High concern for comparative causal inference because 17/52 entered the wrong allocation table and arm-closing rules generated uneven groups; masked assessors/analysts do not repair this. No formal RoB/Jadad score.
quality.attrition: 13/52 (25%)missing follow-up: 5 moved, 4 untraceable, 4 declined (often postnatal confinement). Arm follow-up 19/25, 8/12, 12/15. Nonresponders younger (median 20 vs 25.5) and apparently more trauma-symptomatic. 12/39 assessments occurred 37–61 days rather than target 63.
quality.confounding: Three-arm intended sample 35 and full sample 52 are reported separately. Shared controls with linked depression trial must not be counted as independent evidence. No powered efficacy test; differences in clinical medians are not treatment effects.
quality.adverseFindings: One serious adverse event was assault by husband; assignment and treatment relatedness unreported. Two obstructed/prolonged-labour complications among 29 delivered. Independent assessors found risk/confidentiality discussions needed improvement, and some providers did not respond to IPV disclosure.
quality.transferLimits: Rural Amharic-speaking pregnant women with depressive symptoms and IPV; imminent risk/psychosis/emergency care excluded. No long-term follow-up, no established adolescent subgroup effect.

title: Evaluation of an integrated intervention to reduce psychological distress and intimate partner violence in refugees: Results from the Nguvu cluster randomized feasibility trial.
interventionFamily: Nguvu integrated psychological and violence-prevention intervention.

relevance.population: Congolese refugee women with past-year IPV and elevated psychological distress.
relevance.exposureEvidence: Past-year physical/sexual IPV on Abuse Assessment Screen plus elevated distress; married/in relationship in past 12 months. Psychological-only IPV did not independently meet entry criteria.
relevance.rationale: Explicit domestic/intimate-partner violence exposure in the studied population; psychological intervention is within Language scope.
relevance.transferLimit: See limitation and quality fields; no population-wide clinical recommendation is implied.

age.reportedRange: Eligibility 18+; sample mean 33.52 (SD 9.01) years. Observed minimum/maximum not established.
age.youthScope: No under 18 eligibility; no adolescent subgroup inference.

setting: Nyarugusu refugee camp, Tanzania; Congolese women recruited through local women’s groups, April–September 2017.

sampleSize.description: 43 groups randomized before individual recruitment; 311 enrolled women assigned 158 Nguvu/153 usual care. Follow-up 275 (143/132); adjusted main model 272 and completer analysis 219. Target 400 was not achieved. Narrative and Table 1 reverse cluster-arm counts; retain 43 total and flag discrepancy.

intervention.description: Nguvu integrates shortened cognitive processing therapy with advocacy counselling, adapted for refugee women.
intervention.dose: One individual plus seven weekly group sessions; groups 6–13, facilitated in pairs. Mean 5.4/8 attended; 92/158 (58.2%)completed≥6, 47/158 all 8, 13/158 none.
intervention.provider: Trained nonspecialist Congolese refugee incentive workers with prior basic psychosocial/protection experience.

comparator: Information about existing protection/mental-health services and usual humanitarian case management/referrals; Nguvu participants could also access these services.

outcomes.name: Psychological distress: depression, anxiety, PTSD
outcomes.followUp: Nine weeks after enrollment, approximately one week after intervention
outcomes.result: Baseline-adjusted randomized complete-case estimates do not clearly exclude no benefit; apparent unadjusted differences attenuate.
outcomes.uncertainty: Cluster mixed models adjust demographics and baseline outcome imbalance; PTSD upperCI rounded to 0.00. Not evidence of a definitive efficacy effect.

outcomes.name: Psychological, physical and sexual IPV frequency
outcomes.result: No clear comparative benefit after baseline adjustment.
outcomes.effectEstimate: Log-frequency MD psychological 0.10 (95% CI−0.04, 0.24); physical 0.09 (−0.03, 0.21); sexual−0.03 (−0.24, 0.17).
outcomes.uncertainty: Positive values favor usual care; all intervals include zero. These are log-transformed frequency outcomes, not risk ratios.

outcomes.name: Functional impairment
outcomes.result: No clear comparative difference.
outcomes.uncertainty: Model 3 n 272.

outcomes.name: Exploratory high-baseline-IPV subgroup
outcomes.result: Higher subsequent IPV frequency reported with Nguvu among women above the baseline IPV median.
outcomes.uncertainty: Underpowered moderator tests, multiple comparisons, baseline imbalance and differential completion; a signal to retain, not established treatment-caused harm.

outcomes.name: PTSD among intervention completers
outcomes.result: Selected completer analysis favored Nguvu; it must not replace the randomized comparison.
outcomes.uncertainty: Treatment completion associated with baseline IPV severity; per-protocol comparison is vulnerable to selection bias.

finding: Nguvu was feasible for some refugee women, but the adjusted randomized comparison does not clearly establish psychological or IPV benefit. Severe IPV predicted lower completion; an exploratory subgroup showed higher subsequent IPV. No long-term durability was tested.
limitation: Under-recruitment, baseline imbalances, recruitment after cluster assignment, unmasked self-report, vulnerable assessor masking, complete-case analysis and severity-related intervention dropout limit causal inference. Table 1 reverses the narrative cluster-arm counts; all 43 clusters and individual 158/153 totals are retained.

design.type: Cluster randomized feasibility trial with recruitment after cluster allocation
design.randomizationEvidence: Independent investigator used unrestricted Stata 14 random sequence to allocate all 43 women’s groups simultaneously, then recruited individual women by cluster assignment. Narrative says 21 Nguvu/22 usual-care clusters; Table 1 labels the reverse. Individual allocations 158/153 are consistent.

masking.assessors: Not informed of allocation, but familiar with Nguvu and could infer it from participants at endline; integrity not established.

design.crossRationale: Cluster randomization verified; participants/providers unmasked and assessor masking vulnerable. One cross describes randomized design, not low risk of bias or efficacy.

quality.riskOfBias: Important concerns from baseline mental-health/IPV imbalance, post-allocation recruitment, unmasked self-report and possible assessor unmasking; no formal numeric rating.
quality.attrition: 36/311 (11.6%) lacked endline: 15/158 Nguvu, 21/153 usual care. Eighteen relocated/resettled. Later resettlement stages predicted loss. One withdrew fearing neighbors would learn of participation. Intervention completion 92/158 is distinct from study follow-up 143/158.
quality.confounding: Models 1–3 labeled ITT by authors are complete-case randomized-group comparisons, not all 311 participants. Model 3 controls baseline imbalances; favorable per-protocol PTSD estimate is selected. Moderator tests are exploratory, multiple and underpowered.
quality.adverseFindings: Three adverse events reviewed by DSMB/IRB were judged unlikely due to participation and consistent with ongoing IPV; participants were connected to services. Exploratory high-baseline-IPV group had higher subsequent IPV frequency with Nguvu; not causal proof. One privacy-related withdrawal.
quality.transferLimits: Adult Congolese women in established refugee groups with past-year physical/sexual IPV and elevated distress. Imminent suicidality/severe psychiatric impairment excluded; no durability beyond nine weeks.

title: A Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing HOPE Treatment and Present-Centered Therapy in Women Residing in Shelter with PTSD from Intimate Partner Violence.

relevance.population: Women residing in domestic-violence shelters with IPV-related PTSD.
relevance.exposureEvidence: At least one SVAW or PMWI IPV event in month before shelter entry and full DSM-IV-TR IPV-related PTSD by CAPS were required.
relevance.rationale: Explicit domestic/intimate-partner violence exposure in the studied population; psychological intervention is within Language scope.
relevance.transferLimit: See limitation and quality fields; no population-wide clinical recommendation is implied.

age.youthScope: No child or adolescent participants in reported sample.

setting: Six domestic-violence shelters in five Midwestern US counties; data collected February 2013–February 2017.

sampleSize.description: HOPE 83 versus PCT+ 89. ITT models use all available observations, not complete follow-up for 172. Follow-up counts 154, 142, 135, 127 at post-shelter, post-treatment, 6 and 12 months; outcome-specific denominators vary.

intervention.description: Empowerment-oriented, present-centered CBT with safety planning, cognitive restructuring and coping/relationship skills; current symptoms are linked to IPV but traumatic memories are not processed.
intervention.dose: Up to 16 sessions of 50–60 minutes during shelter and first 3 months after leaving; HOPE mean 8.86 sessions (SD 6.17), 44.2% attended at least 8. Eleven participants across arms received optional shelter boosters.
intervention.provider: Four masters-level therapists trained in both protocols, practice cases and continuing supervision; external sampled fidelity ratings.

comparator: Attention-matched PCT+ with present-focused problem solving, psychoeducation and safety planning, up to 16 sessions; mean 10.06 (SD 5.82). Both groups also received standard shelter services.

outcomes.name: CAPS PTSD severity and IPV measures
outcomes.result: Both active arms improved, but no significant between-group difference at any occasion or in change from baseline.
outcomes.effectEstimate: Reported absolute between-group standardized differences≤0.32 at occasions and≤0.30 for change; no comparative confidence interval provided in the main-report results.
outcomes.uncertainty: No inactive control; null superiority tests do not establish equivalence or isolate therapy from shelter/time effects.

outcomes.name: Reliable PTSD improvement and diagnosis
outcomes.result: Post-treatment reliable CAPS improvement 54/65 (83.1%)HOPE versus 59/77 (76.6%)PCT+; group difference not significant. PTSD diagnosis rates also did not significantly differ at follow-up.
outcomes.uncertainty: These are assessed-participant denominators, not 172 randomized participants.

outcomes.name: Depression, empowerment, posttraumatic cognitions and health-related quality of life
outcomes.result: Within-group improvements without significant comparative superiority.
outcomes.uncertainty: Some residual depression, subthreshold PTSD and abuse remained. Multiple comparisons used alpha<.01.

finding: HOPE did not outperform an attention-matched PCT+ intervention on PTSD, IPV or secondary outcomes. Both active groups improved; no untreated control supports an absolute treatment-effect estimate.
limitation: Treatment providers knew protocols, and shared shelters permit contamination. Participant masking identity is not explicitly role-confirmed despite double-blind labeling. Missing-at-random models assume an unproven missingness mechanism; only 127/172 remained at 12 months. Active-comparator null results are not equivalence evidence.

design.type: Randomized active-comparator trial; author describes double-blind, but only assessor masking is explicitly role-verified
design.randomizationEvidence: Urn randomization assigned 83 toHOPE and 89 toPCT+, stratifying substance-use diagnosis and medication status. Allocation-concealment implementation is not separately established from the report.

masking.participants: Author calls trial double-blind and describes all treatment as HOPE for blinding, identical workbook naming with arm-specific content, and discouraging sharing. These are allocation-identity concealment procedures; the participant role is not separately explicitly confirmed and masking success is unmeasured.
masking.providers: Therapists trained in and delivered both distinct protocols; provider masking is not supported.
masking.assessors: Graduate psychology assessors explicitly masked to treatment condition at follow-up.
masking.analysts: Not established from accessed full report.

design.crossRationale: Retain one cross: randomization and assessor masking verified. Reported double-blind label plus common naming does not independently verify the participant masking role. A two-cross proposal requires further role-specific primary confirmation; successful masking measurement is a separate limitation.

quality.riskOfBias: Randomization and masked clinical assessment strengthen comparison. Therapist allegiance/performance effects, possible contamination, unverified participant-role masking and follow-up attrition remain. No formal RoB or Jadad score assigned.
quality.attrition: Assessment retention 154/172 post-shelter, 142/172 post-treatment, 135/172 at 6 months, 127/172 at 12 months. At 12 months 56/83 HOPE and 71/89 PCT+ contributed CAPS data. Treatment dropout 6/83 versus 5/89 is distinct from missing assessments. Black participants more often completed all assessments than White participants (81.6% vs 62.5%, p=.008).
quality.confounding: ITT multivariate models use all available data under missing-at-random assumption; robust SEs and alpha<.01. Significant within-group change cannot separate psychotherapy, shelter services and time.
quality.adverseFindings: Authors report no study-related serious adverse events, not zero adverse events overall. Ten participants were removed from assigned treatment for higher/different care: 6 HOPE, 4 PCT+; still invited to follow-up. Residual symptoms and some further abuse persisted.
quality.transferLimits: Women with recent IPV and diagnosed PTSD in US shelters; severe suicidal intent/plan, current psychosis, recent substance dependence, bipolar disorder or concurrent individual therapy were excluded.

title: Two-year follow up of a cluster randomised controlled trial for women experiencing intimate partner violence: effect of screening and family doctor-delivered counselling on quality of life, mental and physical health and abuse exposure.

relevance.population: Women who screened positive for fear of a partner in the preceding year.
relevance.exposureEvidence: Women screened positive for fear of a partner/ex-partner in previous 12 months, supplied safe contact/address and could speak English. Screened fear need not equal a specified physical-IPV diagnosis.
relevance.rationale: Explicit domestic/intimate-partner violence exposure in the studied population; psychological intervention is within Language scope.
relevance.transferLimit: See limitation and quality fields; no population-wide clinical recommendation is implied.

age.reportedRange: Eligibility 16–50 years. Baseline table reports 17–29, 30–39, 40–50 year categories; mean 38.5 (SD 8.1). Exact enrolled minimum and under 18 count not established.
age.youthScope: Eligibility included 16–17 years; no adolescent-specific efficacy analysis established.

setting: Victorian Australian primary care, one doctor per practice; doctors recruited 2008–2010.

sampleSize.description: Same 52 doctor-cluster cohort as 2013; 24-month respondents 81/137 intervention and 85/135 control. Longitudinal models used available data for all baseline participants, so 166 is final time point count, not a new trial.

intervention.description: Woman-centered family-doctor counselling using active listening, motivational interviewing and problem solving, supporting the woman’s readiness and decisions.
intervention.dose: Offered 1–6 free sessions over 6 months. 67/137 (49%)attended any; most attended one. Doctor training 6 hours distance learning plus 1 hour practice visit.
intervention.provider: Intervention family doctors, trained for the study.

comparator: Usual primary care; both groups’ doctors received basic IPV information and women received resource lists.

outcomes.name: SF-12 mental health and quality of life

finding: At 24 months the WEAVE counselling offer did not improve primary or secondary outcomes versus usual care. The 12-month secondary depression finding did not persist; these reports are one cohort.
limitation: Only 166/272 responded at 24 months and 49% of women offered counselling attended any (mostlyone session). Self-reported outcomes were unmasked. The absence of statistical benefit is not equivalence; within-group improvement does not establish counselling efficacy.

quality.attrition: 24-monthresponse 81/137 (59%)intervention and 85/135 (63%)control, 166/272 overall. Available-data mixed models do not remove potential nonresponse bias.
quality.confounding: Mixed-effects models use available repeated observations, adjusted for practice clustering and urban/rural stratification. Nonattender exclusions are selected analyses. Both arms received information/resources and repeated IPV questionnaires.
quality.adverseFindings: Report says no significant harms detected and refers to the dedicated harms analysis. A same-family primary abstract nevertheless describes short-/long-term negative emotions, recall, retraumatization and minimization. These are participation experiences, not demonstrated treatment-caused excess harm; counts and causal attribution unavailable. 24-month VAS difference nonsignificant.
